anti_overlap: Do not address whether the PRD's domain ontology is right (a different track owns ontology critique)
Do not address the F2 aggregation operator design as such — focus only on whether the aggregation rule, once written, is *readable by successors*

Focus on the RECORD-KEEPING / INHERITABILITY question: do the artifacts (decision documents AND the event-log stratification scheme they specify) carry their semantics in themselves, or in the heads of the people who produced them?
decision_lens: F4b tags identity-constitutive events at write time and exempts them from compaction past warm. But who decides at write time which event is identity-constitutive? F3's recognition test only fires retroactively — the moment you need to recover identity. A khipukamayuq would ask: when a new operator inherits the event-log five years from now, can they tell from the artifact alone which events are identity-constitutive, or does that classification live in the head of the person who wrote the F3 decision document? If the latter, the stratification is fiber-without-twist — durable-looking, semantically empty.
distance_rationale: No PRD reviewer would consult Andean fiber-record practice when evaluating an event-log compaction policy, because khipu are filed under 'pre-Columbian artifact' or 'anthropology' rather than 'durable-record-keeping system engineering' — yet the khipukamayuq tradition is humanity's most rigorous experiment in whether a compressed record-keeping system can survive the change of operators, because the entire Inca apparatus depended on it AND because the colonial transition tested it in the harshest possible way (almost all khipukamayuq were killed; the surviving knots have been only partially re-decoded). Their answer about what must be encoded in the artifact versus what can live in operator memory is directly the answer F4b needs.
expected_isomorphisms: Both khipu and F4b face the structural problem: a record-keeping system whose entries are compressed (warm-summary / subsidiary-knot) and tiered (hot/warm/cold / cord-position) needs the *classification rule* (which entries are identity-constitutive / which knots are primary) to be encoded in the artifact itself, not in the encoder's head — otherwise the system breaks the moment operators change. The khipukamayuq solution was a structural one: knot-type, twist-direction, and cord-position carry the meta-semantics, so any successor reading the artifact can derive the entry's role from the artifact alone. F4b's analogous question is whether identity-constitutive-ness is structurally derivable (predicate over event kind) or only conventionally tagged (judgement by current author). The Quechua case shows what happens when the answer is the latter and operators change: partial, lossy, irreversible decay of meaning — exactly the failure mode the PRD's 'no re-litigation' goal must avoid.
focus: Whether F4's event-log stratification (hot/warm/cold with selective compaction) and F3's identity-constitutive event class together constitute a durable record-keeping system whose compaction operations are recoverable from the artifact itself, or merely a write-time tagging convention whose meaning evaporates as soon as the operators who set the tags are gone.
name: fd-quipu-knot-stratification
persona: Apply the perspective of a Quechua khipukamayuq — an Inca knot-record specialist responsible for state-scale administrative encoding in fiber across a continent-sized empire without writing. They care about whether a compressed record can be re-read by a successor who never witnessed its creation; they measure durability by whether a knot's *type* (primary, subsidiary, terminal), *position* (cord level, distance-from-spine), and *direction* (S-twist vs Z-twist) carry their semantics in the artifact itself rather than in the encoder's memory; they flag any record-keeping system where the meaning of an entry depends on knowledge not encoded in the entry, because that system fails the first time it changes hands.
review_areas: Whether F4b's write-time tagging of identity-constitutive events specifies an inheritable *classification rule* (so a successor can re-derive the tagging from the event kind alone) or only a *classification act* (the current author tags by judgement, and successors must trust the prior tagging without being able to verify it)

Whether F3's named candidate event kinds (PersonalityScar, formative goal changes, archetype crossings) constitute a closed list (primary knots, terminal knots — types fixed by the system) or an open category that will accrete additions, each addition silently reclassifying past events

Whether F4b's 'summary' of a warm event is a *self-describing compression* (a successor can read the summary and know what was lost) or a *lossy projection* whose lossiness is invisible from the summary alone — khipu summary-knots encode the *operation* that produced them, not just the result

Whether the migration path for existing palettice-sqlite event logs preserves the *creation-context* of each pre-stratification event (was this event written before or after F3's contract landed?) — because retroactively classifying events into a scheme they predate is the failure mode that ends record-keeping traditions

Whether F4a's selective cache invalidation, which uses DerivationDecl.reads, has any analogue protection: when a derivation is invalidated, is the *reason* recorded in a way that lets a successor reconstruct why this entry was invalidated then rather than now? Without that, invalidation history becomes another silent dependency on operator memory

Whether the PRD's central claim — that the four artifacts let a *future* migration team execute 'without re-litigating any of the four questions' — is testable: would a khipukamayuq-equivalent test (hand the four artifacts to someone who has never spoken to the author, ask them to predict the migration's behaviour in a novel edge case) actually pass?

severity_examples.condition: if F3's identity-constitutive event class is enumerated rather than predicated, and F4b consumes the enumeration rather than the predicate, every new event kind is a fresh judgement call that can retroactively erode existing Souls' continuity
severity_examples.scenario: F4b ships with identity-constitutive events tagged at write time by the *current* developer's judgement, with no inheritable classification rule. Two years into the Culture-game era, a new contributor adds a new SoulEvent kind (say, SublimingProximity). They have no way to determine from F3's decision document whether SublimingProximity events should be tagged identity-constitutive — F3 enumerated PersonalityScar, formative goal changes, archetype crossings as examples but did not specify the *property* that makes an event identity-constitutive. The contributor guesses; subsequent compaction either preserves or destroys identity depending on the guess, silently

severity_examples.condition: if the summary format does not encode its own compression ratio and the operation that produced it, the warm tier is a one-way door that no successor can read accurately
severity_examples.scenario: F4b's 'summary' of warm events is specified by giving examples ('a sequence of routine facet-touches becomes a single tendency-summary') rather than by giving the inverse: what a summary must preserve so that the *omission* of detail is itself encoded. A khipu summary-knot carries the count and the operation; F4b's summaries may carry only the result, making it impossible for a successor reading only the warm tier to know whether what they are reading is one event or a thousand

severity_examples.condition: if pre-F4 events are not explicitly classified into the new stratification scheme at migration time (even if the classification is 'unknown, treat as warm-by-default'), the log becomes archaeologically opaque at the boundary
severity_examples.scenario: The migration path for existing palettice-sqlite events (acceptance criterion: 'can either be migrated to the new schema or stays unstratified') treats the two options as equivalent, but they are not: an unstratified pre-F4 log mingled with a stratified post-F4 log creates a record-keeping system with two incommensurable strata, and no rule in F4b for how to read across the boundary. A successor encountering events from 'before the contract' has no protocol

severity_examples.condition: if F3 and F4b do not share a single source-of-truth predicate for identity-constitutive events, the contract between them is structurally fragile
severity_examples.scenario: F3's 'recognition test' is defined per-Soul as a property-based assertion, but the assertion's *grounds* (which events count as recognition-grounding) overlap with F4b's identity-constitutive event class without being explicitly the same set. If they drift apart over time — F3 says 'recognition requires event X' while F4b has already compacted X away as non-constitutive — the recognition test fails silently and the yangsi claim becomes false retroactively

severity_examples.condition: if decision documents are mutable artifacts rather than append-only with explicit succession links, the audit trail for irreversible commitments is broken
severity_examples.scenario: The brainstorm Decisions table is updated to record the chosen extraction shape (F1 acceptance criterion), but no protocol is specified for what happens when a future strategy step revisits F1 — e.g., the cutover trigger fires (workspace → published crate) and the decision document needs to evolve. A khipukamayuq would insist that the original khipu and the revised one *both* be preserved, with the relationship between them encoded; without such a protocol, decision documents become a single mutable cell whose history is gone

source_domain: Quechua khipu administrative knot-record practice as maintained by Inca khipukamayuq specialists (~1400-1572 CE) — a state-scale record-keeping system that encoded census data, tribute schedules, calendrical observations, and (per recent epigraphic work) probably narrative content, using only fiber, knot type, knot position, cord level, colour, and twist direction, sustained across a multi-million-person empire for ~150 years and partially decoded centuries after the last khipukamayuq died
success_hints: Apply the khipukamayuq test: hand the four artifacts (F1-F4 decision documents) to someone who has never spoken to the author and ask them to classify a novel SoulEvent kind. If they cannot, the classification rule is in the author's head, not the artifact

Look for the difference between *enumeration* (a list of items) and *predication* (a property that determines membership). F3's identity-constitutive event class must be a predicate that F4b can apply to events the predicate's author never imagined

Treat every compaction operation as a record-keeping operation in its own right: the summary must encode what it summarised (count, range, operation) so that the lossiness is legible from the artifact
Insist on append-only succession for decision documents: when F1's cutover trigger fires, the new decision should reference and supersede the old, not overwrite it

Use Quechua categorical-knots-versus-numerical-knots distinction: events that contribute to *category* (identity, archetype crossing) are structurally distinct from events that contribute to *count* (routine facet-touches). F4b should make this structural rather than judgmental
task_context: Reviewing a PRD that decomposes the shadow-work migration epic into four features, the fourth of which (F4) introduces hot/warm/cold event-log stratification with identity-constitutive events exempted from compaction past warm. The PRD's central claim is that closing F1-F4 produces four artifacts that let the migration team execute 'without re-litigating any of the four questions' — i.e., the decisions are durable across the operator change between planning and execution. The review goal is to surface whether the artifacts are genuinely self-describing or whether their meaning depends on operator memory that will not transfer.
